newsitem.title: UK: Rain problem for UK grains as harvest approaches.
newsitem.headline: Rain problem for UK grains as harvest approaches.

text.p: Wet weather, which has made such a mess of Britain's sporting calendar, could also hit the yield and quality achieved by the new cereals crop, traders and analysts said.
Concern over too much moisture follows months of worries over not enough, after the driest start to the year since 1929, was seen then as a threat to yields.
"If it keeps on like this it could be very bad," one farming source said. "If it stops raining today and gets sunny it could be a good one," he said.
By midnight on Wednesday the London Weather Centre had recorded 84 millimeters of rain so far in June, almost double the 45.4 millimeter average.

The most pressing problem is for barley, analysts said. Traders fear that the wet could cut quality and there is concern that much of the crop is laying down, because of the rain, making harvesting more difficult.
Barley harvesting should get under way in three or four weeks, farming sources said, although analysts reckoned there may be some coming off much earlier than that.

Wheat is mainly in the dull ripe stage. "If it goes on like this yields will be affected first and then Hagberg," an expert at the ADAS agricultural advisory service said, referring to the Hagberg measure of quality.
The harvest would also be likely to suffer. Even if the weather turns fine, soil moisture was well up, he said. This was likely to mean heavy dews for some time, he said.

Wheat harvesting is due to start around mid-August, the farming source said. "A lot of people are saying their crops don't look as good from close up as from the roadside," he said. "You can't really tell that much until it's coming off."
